newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Insurers could be a casualty in tobacco wars.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Insurers could be a casualty in tobacco wars.

text.p: The insurance industry is growing increasingly worried that it could be among the casualties should tobacco companies suffer costly losses in their legal battles in smoking-related lawsuits.
"I think it's like an inching toward the realisation that there's some potential (for losses)," an industry source said.
Part of the reason is that tobacco settlement negotiations and smoking-related lawsuits may help push the insurance industry's day of reckoning a little closer, he said.
"That would quicken the pace that the insurance industry would have to respond to this kind of issue," the source said.
Most in the industry still believe the chances of a major insured loss is slim, but the stakes are so high and the future so unpredictable that the threat is hard to ignore.
One industry watchdog voiced concern this month that insurers could be forced to participate in any negotiated settlement between the government and the tobacco industry.
The tobacco industry is in the midst of talks with state attorneys general about a settlement to litigation that some reports say could reach $300 billion over 25 years.
"If you presume the insurance industry's share of this $300 billion is just 5 percent, that would be $15 billion," said Standard & Poor's managing director Alan Levin.
Other industry experts said they believe it may just be a matter of time before tobacco companies begin to sue their insurers for coverage.

"At some point in time, when the pain levels hits the right threshold, they're going to start to lean on their insurers," said Michael Flaharty, a New York-based partner in Coopers & Lybrand's national claims consulting practice.
Some policyholders have already given their insurers notice that they want to preserve their right to request coverage in the future, he said.
In March, Louisiana's attorney general named more than 100 insurers as defendants in a lawsuit seeking to recover medical costs.
Insurers argue that policies sold to tobacco companies after the mid-1960s specifically exclude payment for losses related to the harmful effects of smoking.

"Based on discussions with numerous officials in the industry, it appears that the policies that insurers have written over the last 30-plus years have contained an absolute exclusion for tobacco liability," Levin said.
"Thus, insurers' direct liability on those policies from the manufacturers of tobacco products is likely to be very slight," he said.
But insurers cannot be sure those exclusions will hold up in court, others said.
Insurers were forced to pay out on some policies that contained similar asbestos exclusions, Flaharty said.
"For years there have been specific exclusions to asbestos and hazardous waste," Flaharty said. "And yet, insureds will make the claim.
"At the very least, the insurance industry is going to have to defend its position, which in the case of anything that's a mass tort, it's an expensive proposition," he said.

Insurers are also likely to face claims from policyholders who worked with the tobacco industry to produce and sell cigarettes, such as paper manufacturers and advertisers. Policies sold to those parties do not contain tobacco exclusions.

However, in a recent survey of chief financial officers of property-casualty insurance companies, most expressed little concern that mass torts such as tobacco will impose costs on the industry of the magnitude of asbestos and pollution.

But tobacco was singled out as having the most potential to emerge as a significant mass tort liability for the industry in the future, according to the survey, released by the American Academy of Actuaries in March.
Few chief financial officers believe tobacco will be significant for their company.
But the potential magnitude of the tobacco industry's losses and the unpredictability of the U.S. courts is enough to make some corners of the insurance industry a little nervous.
"It's an issue that's being watched very carefully," Salomon Brothers analyst Michael Smith said.
"I think the concern lies with what might happen in the courts," he said. "If court decisions start breaking in the wrong way then it becomes a problem," he said.
Industry sources said it was still too early to know how much those losses eventually could be.
"What is it? Who knows? It could be the moon or it could be a big fizzle," said Flaharty.
